questions.q: You must refactor a 300-line checkout function that runs in production and has no tests. What should you do before moving any code?
questions.explain: A characterization test pins current behaviour, right or wrong. Every refactoring step can then be checked against it. Without it, a changed total or a missing e-mail goes unnoticed until a customer reports it.
options: Split it into classes so it is easier to test later
Write characterization tests that record what it does today for a few real inputs
Rewrite it from scratch in a new file and switch over
Add interfaces for every dependency it uses

questions.q: After extracting priceOrder, a characterization test fails: the old code returned 145125 kobo, the new function returns 145124. What does this tell you?
questions.explain: A refactoring must not change behaviour. One kobo on every order is real money and a real difference between the receipt and the charge. If the new rounding is actually better, that is a behaviour change to agree on and ship on its own, not a side effect of moving code.
options: The old code was wrong and the test should be deleted
Characterization tests are too strict for refactoring
The refactoring changed behaviour (probably rounding). Find out why, then either restore the old result or change it deliberately in a separate, reviewed step
Nothing, one kobo is within rounding error

questions.q: The tangled placeOrder validates, prices, charges, saves and e-mails. Which part is the safest and most useful to extract first?
questions.explain: Pure code can be moved and tested without fakes, databases or networks. Once it is out, the remaining function is mostly side effects in a clear order, which is easier to handle next.
options: The payment call, because it is the riskiest
The e-mail, because it is the shortest
Validation and pricing, because they are pure calculations that need nothing from the outside world
The database write, because it holds the most data

questions.q: Which of these best describes a concern in "separation of concerns"?
questions.explain: Pricing, payment, storage and notification are concerns: each has its own experts and its own reasons to change. Separating them means a pricing change does not touch the payment code.
options: A single line of code
Any function longer than 20 lines
One area of knowledge the code needs, which one expert or team could own and would ask to change
A bug that someone is worried about

questions.q: Which module description signals low cohesion?
questions.explain: If you need "and" to describe a module, its parts serve different purposes and change for different reasons. Such modules become merge-conflict magnets and hide duplicates.
options: "Computes order prices from lines, coupons and VAT"
"Stores orders in PostgreSQL"
"Formats naira amounts and validates e-mails and retries failed calls"
"Sends order notifications by e-mail"

questions.q: VAT is computed in the checkout, the invoice and the receipt. The rate changes and only the receipt is updated, so receipts disagree with charges. What is the design problem?
questions.explain: High cohesion means one idea lives in one place. When the invoice and the receipt call priceOrder, they cannot disagree with the charge, whatever the rate becomes.
options: The VAT rate should be a let instead of a literal
One idea ("how a total is computed") has no single home: low cohesion. All three should ask one pricing module
The receipt should not show VAT at all
The three files should be merged into one big file

questions.q: Four modules import an exported array outbox and push to it or clear it. Which kind of coupling is this, and why does it hurt?
questions.explain: Shared mutable globals connect every user of them. Tests that run in the same process see each other's leftovers, and you cannot tell who emptied the array.
options: Data coupling; it is the best kind
Global (common) coupling: any module can change shared state, so a bug in one can break the others, and tests leak state into each other
Stamp coupling: too much data is passed
Control coupling: a flag chooses the code path

questions.q: notify(order, true) sends an SMS; notify(order, false) sends an e-mail. What is the better design?
questions.explain: A flag that picks the code path is control coupling: the caller must know how the callee is built inside. A string flag is the same coupling with a different type. Passing the behaviour itself (a notifier) lets new channels be added without editing notify.
options: Use a string "sms" instead of true; that removes the coupling
Pass the notifier to use (an object with send), or have two clearly named functions, so the caller does not steer the callee's internal branches
Keep it; boolean parameters are the simplest option
Make notify read a global setting instead

questions.q: The e-mail function receives the whole order record, including the card number, although it only needs the address and the total. What is the risk?
questions.explain: Passing only what is needed (data coupling) keeps modules independent of each other's record shapes and limits where sensitive data can leak.
options: None, passing more data is always more flexible
It makes the program slower
Stamp coupling: the e-mail code now depends on the order's shape, and sensitive fields travel to code (and logs, and templates) that should never see them
TypeScript will refuse it

questions.q: A function does const client = new PaystackClient(KEY) inside itself before charging. Which problem does this cause first?
questions.explain: A function that builds its own collaborators has decided for every caller, tests included. Receiving the gateway as a parameter (dependency injection) moves that decision to the composition root.
options: It is slower than a global client
No test can run it without the real provider, and switching providers means editing the function
TypeScript cannot type the client
The key will be logged

questions.q: A developer makes status private and adds setStatus(value) that assigns any status. Is the order encapsulated now?
questions.explain: Encapsulation is about protecting invariants. Methods such as markPaid and markRefunded check the current state; a general setter checks nothing.
options: Yes, the field is private
No. Any code can still set any status in any order; the rules (only a paid order can be refunded) are still not enforced anywhere
Yes, because setters are slower to call
No, because private fields do not work with getters

questions.q: Which of these is an invariant of an order?
questions.explain: An invariant is a rule that must be true of the object at every moment. Freezing the lines and computing the price inside Order.create makes this one impossible to break.
options: The order was created on a weekday
The total always equals the price of the order's lines after discount plus VAT
The customer has placed an order before
The e-mail was delivered

questions.q: Why does the lesson's Order have a private constructor and a static create method?
questions.explain: Controlling creation is part of encapsulation: every order that exists went through the one door that establishes the invariants.
options: Because TypeScript classes cannot have public constructors with parameter properties
So the only way to get an order is through create, which always computes the price from frozen lines; no caller can build an order with a mismatched total
To make orders singletons
To hide the class from other modules

questions.q: Which payment interface is a leaky abstraction?
questions.explain: Returning the provider's own field names forces the caller to understand one provider's format. A second provider with different fields silently breaks the caller, as the Flutterwave example showed.
options: charge(card, amountKobo, reference): Promise<{ ok: true; chargeId } | { ok: false; reason }>
charge(request): Promise<{ status: boolean; data: { gateway_response: string } }>, returning the provider's raw answer
refund(chargeId): Promise<void>
charge(amountKobo): Promise<string> that throws on decline

questions.q: Who should decide the shape of the PaymentGateway interface?
questions.explain: The side that uses an abstraction knows what it needs: did it work, a reference for refunds, and whether a failure is retryable. Designing from the provider's side leaks the provider into the service.
options: The payment provider's SDK
The code that uses it (the order service), in its own words; each provider then gets a translator to that shape
The database layer
Whoever writes the first implementation

questions.q: The card was charged, then saving the order fails because the database is down. What should the order service do?
questions.explain: The charge cannot be rolled back like a database transaction, so an explicit undo step (a compensation) is needed. Otherwise the customer has paid for an order the shop does not know about.
options: Return success; the payment went through
Retry the charge
Compensate: refund the charge, mark the order refunded, and report the failure
Nothing; the database will come back

questions.q: The order is paid and saved, but the e-mail server is down. Where does the lesson put the decision "do not fail the order because of this"?
questions.explain: It is a policy about notifying, not about ordering. As a wrapper it can be applied to any notifier and changed without editing the service.
options: In a try/catch inside every service that sends messages
In a bestEffort wrapper around the notifier, chosen in the composition root
In the e-mail server's configuration
Nowhere; the order should fail

questions.q: Which of these most likely does not need an interface and injection?
questions.explain: Inject what talks to the outside world or must be replaced in tests. A pure function is already easy to test and replace; an interface around it adds names and hides nothing.
options: The payment gateway
The order store
The clock used to decide if a booking is late
A pure priceOrder function with one implementation

questions.q: What is the composition root?
questions.explain: Only the composition root knows every concrete choice: which gateway, which store, which notifiers. Tests have their own small composition roots that pick fakes.
options: The base class every service inherits from
The one place, usually the entry file, that creates the concrete parts and connects them
The first function called in each request
The folder that holds interfaces

questions.q: Which is the most practical everyday measure of whether a design is loosely coupled?
questions.explain: Coupling is about change. If a VAT change touches one file and a provider switch adds one file and edits the composition root, the design is doing its job.
options: The number of classes in the project
The number of interfaces
How many files typical changes touch, for example "change the VAT rate" or "switch payment provider"
The length of the longest function

questions.q: A developer splits a clear 15-line function into seven files of two lines each. Which principle suffers?
questions.explain: Separate by reason to change, not by line count. Over-splitting scatters one concern the same way the VAT rule was scattered.
options: Encapsulation
Cohesion: one idea is now scattered, and reading it means opening seven files
Nothing; smaller files are always better
Composition

questions.q: A PlaceOrderDto only carries values from an HTTP body into the service. Should it be a class with private fields and guarded methods?
questions.explain: Data that only crosses a boundary is checked once (by validation) and then read. The Order has rules about its lifecycle, so it gets the private state and guarded methods.
options: Yes, every type should be encapsulated
No. It has no invariants of its own to protect; a readonly interface is enough. Encapsulation belongs where there are rules
Yes, otherwise JSON.parse will fail
No, because DTOs must be mutable

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The gift function changed the lines from outside, and nothing recomputed the total. The invariant "total matches lines" is broken because any code can mutate the record.
options: 2 undefined

questions.explain: Both the array and the line object are frozen. Pushing to a frozen array always throws a TypeError, and assigning to a property of a frozen object throws in strict mode code (modules and TypeScript output are strict). Nothing changed.
options: false false 2 5

true
true

true

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The methods form a one-way state machine: pending → paid → refunded. Paying a refunded order is refused because the status is no longer pending.
options:
markPaid -> paid
markRefunded -> refunded
markPaid -> paid

markPaid -> paid
markRefunded -> refunded
cannot pay an order that is refunded

markPaid -> paid
cannot refund an order that is paid
cannot pay an order that is paid

cannot pay an order that is pending
markRefunded -> refunded
markPaid -> paid

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With the coupon: 900 after discount, VAT is 67.5, which Math.round turns into 68, so 968. Without: 1000 + 75 = 1075. VAT is charged on the discounted amount.

questions.q: The service was written against Paystack's response. What does this print for a Flutterwave answer?
questions.explain: "success" === true is false, and Flutterwave has no gateway_response field. The provider's details leaked into the check, so an approved payment reads as a failure.
options: true Approved
false Approved
false undefined
true undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The function collects every problem instead of throwing at the first. The items list is not empty, and only RICE has a quantity below 1.
options: [ 'email' ]
[ 'email', 'qty RICE' ]
[ 'email', 'no items', 'qty RICE' ]
[ 'email', 'qty RICE', 'qty OIL' ]

questions.q: Two wrappers around a failing notifier. What does this print?
questions.explain: logged is outside, so it logs first. bestEffort swallows the error, so from logged's point of view the send succeeded and it logs "sent ada", which is misleading. Wrapper order matters.
options: try ada, swallowed
try ada, swallowed, sent ada
swallowed, try ada, sent ada
try ada

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: allOf sends in order and stops at the first error, so the e-mail is never sent. That is why the lesson wraps each channel in bestEffort before combining them.
options:
sms down
1

sms down
0

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The save fails after the charge, so the catch block refunds the charge and returns early. No e-mail is sent for an order that does not exist.
options: ok [ 'charge', 'email' ]
not_saved [ 'charge', 'refund CH-1' ]
not_saved [ 'charge', 'refund CH-1', 'email' ]
not_saved [ 'charge' ]

questions.q: Two modules share one global counter. What does this print?
questions.explain: After the first id, nextId is 2. The import adds 100, so the next id is ORD-102. Any module can change the shared counter, so the id sequence depends on code far away.
options: ORD-1 ORD-2

ORD-1
ORD-2

ORD-1
ORD-102

ORD-1
ORD-101

questions.q: A test passes fakes that record calls. What does it print?
questions.explain: The invalid amount returns before the gateway is touched, which the recorded calls prove. That is exactly the kind of fact a fake makes easy to check.
options: invalid ok [ 'charge 0', 'charge 500', 'save' ]
invalid ok [ 'charge 500', 'save' ]
declined ok [ 'charge 0', 'charge 500', 'save' ]
invalid ok []

questions.q: The function below mixes pricing with side effects. Extract a pure function cartTotalKobo(lines, prices) that returns the subtotal plus 7.5% VAT (rounded with Math.round), and make checkout use it. The program should print 483750 and then charged 483750.
questions.explain: The calculation now has no side effects and takes its price table as a parameter, so it can be tested alone. checkout keeps only its side effect.

questions.q: Write validateTransfer(t) that returns a list of all problems: "amount must be positive whole kobo" if amountKobo is not a positive integer, "cannot transfer to the same account" if from === to, and "account number must be 10 digits" for each of from/to that is not exactly ten digits. The program should print [] and then 3.
questions.explain: Collecting every problem gives the user all the feedback at once, and a pure function like this is tested without a bank. (Reporting the account-number rule once or once per field are both reasonable; this solution reports it once.)

questions.q: Write bestEffort(notifier, log): it returns a notifier whose send calls the wrapped one and, if that throws, calls log with "failed: " + error.message instead of throwing. The program should print failed: sms down and then done.
questions.explain: The wrapper has the same interface as what it wraps, so the service cannot tell the difference. The policy "never fail because of a notification" lives in one small function. Note the await inside try: without it, the rejection would escape the catch.

questions.q: Write a class Account with a private balance (starting at 0), a getter balanceKobo, and methods deposit(kobo) and withdraw(kobo). withdraw must throw new Error("insufficient funds") if the amount is larger than the balance. The program should print 300000, then insufficient funds, then 300000.
questions.explain: The balance can only change through the two methods, and withdraw checks before it changes anything, so a refused withdrawal leaves the balance untouched. A real version would also reject non-positive or fractional amounts.

questions.q: Write toChargeResult(raw) that translates a provider answer into the shop's own shape: { ok: true, chargeId } when raw.status === "success" and raw.data.processor_response === "Approved" (with chargeId taken from raw.data.flw_ref), otherwise { ok: false, reason: "declined" }. The program should print true FLW-12 then false declined.
questions.explain: The provider's field names stay inside this one function. The service only ever sees ok, chargeId and reason, so adding a provider never changes it.

questions.q: Write allOf(...notifiers) that returns one notifier whose send sends to every notifier in order. The program should print email: hi then sms: hi.
questions.explain: The combined notifier has the same interface as each part, so code that expects one notifier accepts the combination. That is composition: new behaviour from existing parts, with no edits to the service.

questions.q: isOverdue reads the real clock, so it cannot be tested reliably. Change it to take a now parameter (a Date) and call it with fixed dates. An invoice due 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z should print false for now = 2026-02-28T12:00:00Z and true for now = 2026-03-02T00:00:00Z.
questions.explain: The clock is part of the outside world, like a database. Passing the time in makes the function pure and its tests repeatable on any day. In a service, you would inject a clock object instead of a date per call.

questions.q: notify(order, true) means SMS and false means e-mail. Remove the flag: make notify(order, channel) take a channel object with a send(text) method, and call it with the two channels given. The program should print sms: ORD-1 paid then email: ORD-1 paid.
questions.explain: The caller no longer steers notify's internal branches with a boolean. A WhatsApp channel can be added without touching notify at all.
questions.expected:
sms: ORD-1 paid
email: ORD-1 paid
